1. **A completion costs less.** With nobody deep, any completion that beats its man can go a long way. But
   on third-and-2 the defense loses the down on almost any completion anyway, so the bet risks less than on
   third-and-10, where a short completion is still a stop and the defense would be giving up its safe
   outcome to gamble.
2. **Every defender is close to the line, which helps against the run.** On third-and-short the offense
   might run; Cover 0 puts eight or nine defenders within a few yards of the ball.

Some coordinators use it at longer distances too, for a third reason: **it forces the decision now.** A
quarterback facing six rushers and no safety has well under two seconds. He must throw hot, against tight
man coverage, before the route has developed. On third-and-2 that hot throw can convert, but on
third-and-6 or 7 the routes fast enough to beat the rush mostly end short of the line. That is the Cover 0
of the film rooms below. Spagnuolo's Chiefs and Flores's Dolphins called it on short third downs like
everyone else, but kept calling it on long ones, where most of the league nearly stops: on third-and-7 or
longer, the 2021 Dolphins played Cover 0 on `{python} pct(MIA21_C07)` of charted dropbacks
(`{python} ordinal(MIA21_C07_RK)` in the NFL; league median `{python} pct(MED21_C07)`), and the 2025 Chiefs on
`{python} pct(KC25_C07)` (`{python} ordinal(KC25_C07_RK)`; median `{python} pct(MED25_C07)`).[^c0long] They were
betting that the hot throw would land short. The league habit (short yardage, for the run and because the
completion converts anyway) and theirs (medium and long, because the completion lands short) are two
answers to the same question: where is the quick completion least damaging?

What it gives up is everything behind it. A Cover 0 blitz that doesn't get home is one broken tackle away
from a touchdown, and offenses that see it coming (both safeties walking down, corners pressed, linebackers
mugged in the A gaps) answer with slants, rubs, and protection that keeps an extra blocker in.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Dolphins 2021 — Brian Flores's third-down zeros"}
Brian Flores spent fifteen seasons in Bill Belichick's New England organisation (four in scouting, then
eleven on the coaching staff) before becoming Miami's head coach (2019–2021), and his Dolphins played Cover 0 more than anyone. In 2020 they played it on
`{python} pct(MIA20_C0)` of charted third-down dropbacks, level with Belichick's Patriots
(`{python} pct(NE20_C0)`) at the top of the league; in 2021 on `{python} pct(MIA21_C0)`, the most in the NFL
and more than four times the league median (`{python} pct(MED21_C0)`).[^mia]

The signature night came on Thursday, November 11, 2021, when the 2–7 Dolphins beat the 6–2 Ravens
`{python} G_HS`–`{python} G_AS` in Miami. Flores sent five or more rushers on
`{python} pct(G_BL)` of Lamar Jackson's `{python} G_N` charted dropbacks and played Cover 0 on
`{python} G_C0` of them, with his safeties walked up as rushers or man defenders, and Baltimore converted
`{python} G3_CONV` of `{python} G3_N` third downs. The Ravens' own columnist described an offense
"overwhelmed by relentless blitzes."[^eisenberg]

**What to notice:** before the snap, count the deep safeties. If there are none, and the corners are
pressed, it is Cover 0 or a disguise of it, and the ball has to come out in well under two seconds. Flores kept
the same idea in Minnesota (he has been the Vikings' defensive coordinator since 2023, and still is in
2026), where the Cover 0 look is as often a disguise as a call.
:::

## Rush three, drop eight

At the other end of the dial is a call that sounds like giving up: **[rush three, drop
eight](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-three-drop-eight)**. Three rushers, eight defenders in
coverage, usually on third-and-long.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-three
#| fig-cap: "Rush three, drop eight on third-and-12 (illustrative). Three linemen rush; a stand-up edge player (B) who looked like a fourth rusher drops instead. Behind them, five underneath defenders sink to 11 to 13 yards, right on the line to gain (orange), and three deep defenders sit at 18 to 21 yards. The offense runs a typical third-and-long pattern: curls at the sticks outside, a dig at 13 from the left slot, and the tight end up the seam to hold the deep middle. Every one of those windows has a defender in it. The offense has five blockers for three rushers, so the center and left guard double the nose and the right guard looks for work, and the back's checkdown is wide open, about 10 yards short."
def rush3_play():
    dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "E"),
           D("OLB", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6, "B"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.5, 0.8, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 6.0, "SS"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=12)
    for k in ("LDE", "NT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-2.0, 0.0)])
    # protection: tackles on the ends, center and left guard double the nose, right guard looks for work
    p.block("LT", pts=[(-1.3, -0.5)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(-1.3, 0.5)])
    p.block("LG", pts=[(-0.8, 0.8)]); p.block("C", pts=[(-0.7, 0.0)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(-1.2, 0.9)])
    p.route("X", r.curl(13.5)); p.route("Z", r.curl(13.5))
    p.route("H", r.dig(14.5, 8)); p.route("Y", r.seam(17))
    p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (2.5, 3.4), (8.0, 3.7)], side=-1)       # check, then release past the line
    zs = (5.0, 7.5)
    p.drop("NB", (12.0, -13.0), zone=zs); p.drop("OLB", (11.5, -6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("MIKE", (13.0, 0.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("SS", (11.5, 6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("DB", (12.0, 13.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("LCB", (18.5, -16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0)); p.drop("RCB", (18.5, 16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0))
    p.drop("FS", (21.0, 0.0), zone=(7.0, 12.0))
    return p


p = rush3_play()
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 27.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, 24.7, -11.0, "five underneath at 11–13 yards:\nevery window at the sticks is filled", fontsize=6.5)
say(fld, p, 24.7, 12.0, "three deep at 18–21 yards:\nnothing gets over the top", fontsize=6.5)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.8, 10.5), (-1.9, 2.5), "three rushers, five blockers: C and LG\ndouble the nose, RG looks for work")
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, -13.5), (3.0, -5.3), "checkdown: open,\nabout 10 yards short")
plt.show()
```

The logic is the sticks defense taken to its limit. On third-and-12 the offense needs a completion past
12 yards, and eight defenders can put a body in every window at that depth and still keep three deep. The
quarterback is offered the checkdown and little else.

The price is **time**. Three rushers against five blockers will rarely get home quickly: the offense has
two spare linemen to double-team the best rusher, and the quarterback can hold the ball for four seconds
or more. Given that long, receivers can run a second route, and a quarterback who can move will find the
gaps in the rush and scramble through them. That is why rush-three calls often come with the next section's
idea attached, a defender assigned to the quarterback, and why defenses mix them with pressure: a quarterback
who sees three rushers on one third-and-long can't assume he'll get time on the next.

How rare is it, and does it work? Across 2023–2025 defenses rushed three or fewer on
`{python} pct(DEF.loc['11+', 'rush3'])` of third-and-11-or-more dropbacks and `{python} pct(DEF.loc['7–10', 'rush3'])`
at 7 to 10. On third-and-7 or longer, offenses converted `{python} pct(RO.loc['3 or fewer', 'conv'])` against
three or fewer rushers, `{python} pct(RO.loc['4', 'conv'])` against four and `{python} pct(RO.loc['5+', 'conv'])`
against five or more.[^rush3] Sack rates run the way you'd expect:
`{python} pct(RO.loc['3 or fewer', 'sack'], 1)` with three rushers, `{python} pct(RO.loc['5+', 'sack'], 1)` with
five or more.

Read those conversion rates carefully, because they seem to say the blitz is the *worst* call on
third-and-long. Most of that is the distance hiding inside the average. Three-man rushes come mostly on the
very longest downs, which are the hardest to convert whatever the defense does, and blitzes mostly at 7 to
10, which are easier. Hold the distance still and the gap nearly closes: on third-and-7 to 10 alone,
offenses converted `{python} pct(RO10.loc['4', 'conv'])` against four rushers and
`{python} pct(RO10.loc['5+', 'conv'])` against five or more. So the blitz doesn't stop third-and-long more
often than a four-man rush, on average. It does change *how* the down ends: more sacks, more hurried throws,
and the occasional receiver left alone. That near-tie is roughly what you'd expect if coordinators are
mixing their calls well. If one call were clearly better, everyone would call it more, offenses would
prepare for it, and its edge would shrink. The blitz earns its place by being one option in a mix the
quarterback can't predict, not by winning every time it is called.

Some defenses lean on it. Brian Flores's 2023 Vikings, the league's heaviest blitzers that season, also
rushed three or fewer on `{python} pct(R3T[2023]['MIN'])` of their third-and-7-or-longer dropbacks, the most in the
NFL: a defense that might send seven or three, from the same look. In 2025 the leaders were Jesse Minter's
Chargers (`{python} pct(R3T[2025]['LAC'])`; Minter is the Ravens' head coach in 2026) and Kelvin Sheppard's
Lions (`{python} pct(R3T[2025]['DET'])`).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: rush three, drop eight"}
**What it solves:** on third-and-long the offense needs a completion past the sticks, so the defense puts
its numbers where the completion has to happen, and accepts a free short throw. **What it gives up:** the
pass rush. With only three rushing, the quarterback gets time, and time eventually beats any coverage. It
works best against quarterbacks who don't run and offenses without a receiver who can turn a checkdown into
twelve yards, and it works only as one call in a mix.
:::

## The spy

The last family answers a problem that third down's own calls create. Drop eight into coverage, or even
seven, and the coverage covers everyone *except* the man with the ball. Play man coverage, and it is
worse: every man defender is running with his receiver, **back turned to the quarterback**, so nobody sees
him take off. (Zone defenders at least face the quarterback and can come up when he runs.) A quarterback
who can run looks downfield, sees every receiver covered, sees the rush lanes open, and goes. Scrambles
were only `{python} pct(SCR_SHARE)` of third-down dropbacks in 2021–2025, but on third-and-7 to 10 they
converted `{python} pct(SCR_CONV_LONG)` of the time, against `{python} pct(DROP_CONV_LONG)` for dropbacks as a
whole.[^scramble] Against the quarterbacks who scramble most, that is a weapon a defense has to plan for.

The defense's answer is the **[spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy)** (or **[QB
spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-spy)**): a defender assigned not to a receiver or a rush lane but to
the quarterback himself. He stands at linebacker depth, usually 5 to 7 yards off the ball and in front of
the quarterback, keeps his eyes on him, and mirrors him. If the quarterback throws, the spy has done
nothing, which is the price. If he runs, the spy meets him.

```{python}
#| label: fig-spy
#| fig-cap: "A spy on third-and-6, 2.3 seconds after the snap (simulated, illustrative; faint lines show where each player has been, dashed arrows where the quarterback and the spy go next). The defense plays Cover 1, man coverage on every receiver who goes out, with one deep safety; it rushes four and assigns the Mike linebacker (purple ring) to the quarterback. The back has stayed in to block, so the Will who had him waits. The man defenders have turned and run with their receivers, backs to the quarterback. The ends have rushed in their lanes, pushing the tackles back from the outside so the quarterback can't escape around them. He steps up toward the B gap (between the left guard and tackle), and the spy, who has shuffled with him from 6 yards, is already closing: he meets him (×) about two yards past the line, short of the line to gain. In an ordinary Cover 1 this Mike might have been the robber; using him as a spy costs the defense that help."
def spy_play():
    dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -5.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 9.5, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
    # routes: outs set a yard and a half past a third-and-6 line (offsets from a 1.5-yard-deep slot)
    p.route("X", r.go(14)); p.route("Z", r.go(14)); p.route("H", r.out(9.0, 4)); p.route("Y", r.out(9.0, 4))
    for dk, ok in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
        p.man(dk, ok)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.8, -4.0, 2.6)], "block")                      # six-man protection: the back stays in
    # the quarterback: drop, hold, then step up toward the left B gap
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.7, -7.0, 0.0), (1.5, -7.0, 0.0), (2.3, -4.0, -2.4)], "run")
    # the line: pass sets; the tackles are pushed back by the ends, the guards and center hold the inside
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.6, -2.0, -4.2), (1.8, -3.3, -4.8), (2.3, -3.6, -5.0)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.6, -1.8, -1.5), (2.3, -2.4, -1.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.6, -1.8, 0.3), (2.3, -2.2, 0.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.6, -1.8, 1.9), (2.3, -2.4, 2.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -2.0, 4.2), (1.8, -3.3, 4.8), (2.3, -3.6, 5.0)], "block")
    # the rush: ends stay outside their tackles (contain), tackles push into the guards
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.6, -0.8, -5.8), (1.8, -2.4, -6.2), (2.3, -2.8, -6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -0.8, 5.8), (1.8, -2.4, 6.2), (2.3, -2.8, 6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.6, -0.6, -0.8), (2.3, -1.1, -0.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.3), (2.3, -1.1, 3.0)], "rush")
    # the spy: shuffles with the quarterback's shoulders, then starts to close
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.5, 6.0, 0.0), (2.0, 5.6, -0.8), (2.3, 4.9, -1.4)], "path")
    p.highlight("MIKE", color=PURPLE)
    return p


spy = spy_play()
T_SPY = 2.3
MEET = (2.1, -3.3)
fld = snapshot(spy, T_SPY, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.5, 18.5), ruler_fs=6.3)
ax = fld.ax
PPs = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*spy.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
at = lambda k: tuple(float(v) for v in spy.position(k, T_SPY))  # noqa: E731
# the next half-second: the quarterback's escape and the spy's angle, and where they meet
for key, end, col, lw in (("QB", (MEET[0] - 0.5, MEET[1]), style.OFFENSE_DARK, 2.4),
                          ("MIKE", (MEET[0] + 0.4, MEET[1] + 0.2), PURPLE, 2.2)):
    x0, y0 = PPs(*at(key)); x1, y1 = PPs(*end)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=12, color=col, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=8, shrinkB=1,
                                 zorder=9))
xm, ym = PPs(*MEET)
ax.plot([float(xm)], [float(ym)], marker="x", ms=10, mew=2.6, color=style.INK, zorder=12)
point_to(fld, spy, (12.4, 6.6), at("MIKE"), "the spy (M): eyes on the\nQB, shuffling, now closing")
point_to(fld, spy, (1.8, -13.5), MEET, "spy meets him here:\n2 yards past the line,\nshort of the sticks", shrink=5)
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, 10.0), at("RDE"), "ends rush in their lanes,\noutside the tackles: contain")
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, -9.5), at("QB"), "quarterback steps up\ntoward the B gap")
point_to(fld, spy, (11.4, -9.2), at("LCB"), "man defenders run with their\nreceivers, backs to the quarterback")
plt.show()
```

Who spies? Someone fast enough to match a running quarterback and big enough to tackle him: usually a
linebacker, sometimes a safety or nickel back against the fastest quarterbacks, occasionally a defensive
lineman who "rushes" by stepping up and sitting in the middle. A linebacker assigned to the back can also
be a *green dog* (some staffs say *hug* or *add-on*), who joins the rush only if the back stays in to
block ([Linebackers and the Second Level](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)).
The spy comes with a rush plan too: against a running quarterback the rushers play a
[mush rush](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mush-rush) (some say *cage rush*), staying square in their
[rush lanes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rush-lane) and pushing the blockers back into the quarterback
instead of racing around them ([The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd)). The ends keep
[contain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contain), the pocket shrinks around him but doesn't open, and the
spy is the last line if he finds a crease anyway.

The trade is the familiar one: the spy is a defender who isn't covering anyone. In Cover 1 he usually
replaces the robber, so the middle of the field loses its best in-cut defender; in zone he is one fewer
underneath player. A spy can also be *used*. Offenses run a receiver right at him to make him choose, or
send the back on a route he has to respect, and a linebacker spying a quarterback who is faster than he is
can be outrun to the sideline. Like every third-down call, it works best as one of several from the same look.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: two spies for Lamar Jackson, 2024 and 2025"}
Lamar Jackson, the most dangerous running quarterback of his era, sees spies as often as anyone, and two
games a year apart show both sides of the bargain.

**Chiefs 2024, opening night (September 5).** Kansas City moved linebacker Leo Chenal all over its front
(in the box, on the defensive line and over the slot) and used him to spy Jackson in key moments,
mirroring him and running him down on scrambles.[^chenal] It didn't
stop the running: Jackson carried `{python} KC24['car']` times for `{python} KC24['yds']` yards, including
`{python} KC24['scr']` scrambles, and on third down he ran `{python} KC24['car3']` times for
`{python} KC24['yds3']` yards and `{python} KC24['conv3']` conversions. The Chiefs won anyway,
`{python} KC24['hs']`–`{python} KC24['as_']`, in a game decided on its final snap.

**Lions 2025, Week 3 (September 22, *Monday Night Football*).** Detroit's coordinator Kelvin Sheppard,
who had earlier said publicly that he didn't like using a spy, built a plan around one and made it hard to find. Jackson ran
`{python} DET25['car']` times for `{python} DET25['yds']` yards, was sacked `{python} DET25['sacks']` times,
and the Lions won in Baltimore, `{python} DET25['as_']`–`{python} DET25['hs']`. Sheppard gave the credit not
to the spy but to the disguise around it: "it's because we're making everything look the same," he said,
"and when you do that, it's impossible to know who's coming, who's the spy, who's in coverage."[^sheppard]

**What to notice:** before a third-and-medium snap against a running quarterback, look for the linebacker
who sits straight in front of him at 5 or 6 yards and doesn't move with any receiver. After the snap,
watch him: a spy shuffles with the quarterback's shoulders. A green-dog rusher who comes forward late is
the same idea, disguised.
:::

## The third-down dial at a glance

Put the chapter's pieces side by side. The distance sets the menu for both sides; the pre-snap picture
tells you which item is likely, but only some calls have a reliable tell, because the defense works hard
to make the rest look alike.

| Distance | Offense's usual tools | Defense's usual calls | What you can see before the snap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short (1–3) | Power run, sneak, quick man-beaters (slant, rub) | Tight man (Cover 1), Cover 0, a packed box | No deep safety, pressed corners, linebackers mugged in the A gaps: Cover 0 or a disguise of it |
| Medium (4–6) | Option routes, mesh, rubs, matchups, empty | Cover 1 with a robber, mugs and disguise, some pressure | One deep safety, defenders tight on receivers; the robber or a mug shows where help is |
| Long (7–10) | Sticks routes past the line, six-man protection, hot throws | Blitz and simulated pressure, 2-Man, sticks zone | Dime personnel; defenders walked up to the line (blitz *or* sim: you usually can't tell which); two deep with tight, inside defenders suggests 2-Man |
| Very long (11+) | Screen, draw, safe completion, a shot | Sticks zone, rush three/drop eight | Six or more defensive backs, soft corners, two or three deep; only three linemen with a hand down hints at rush three |
| Any distance, running QB | Scramble, designed run, routes at the spy | Spy, mush rush | A linebacker in front of the quarterback at 5–7 yards, lined up on nobody |

## Is third down a skill?

Third down feels like the purest test of a team, and it is a big one. But it is also a small sample: a
team faces roughly 200 to 230 third downs a season, and every one is a coin weighted by distance. Two
consequences are worth knowing.

First, **early downs decide a lot of third down.** A team that is on schedule faces third-and-3, not
third-and-9, and converts more often without being any better *at* third down. How do we know? With a
**correlation**, a number between 0 and 1 (for this kind of comparison) that measures how well one
season's figure lines up with the next: 0 means last year tells you nothing about this year, 1 means it
tells you everything, and anything around 0.2 or 0.3 is a weak link, real but swamped by luck. Across
2016–2025, a team's success rate on first and second down predicted its third-down conversion rate the
*next* season (correlation `{python} f"{R_ESR:.2f}"`) nearly as well as its own third-down rate did
(`{python} f"{R_OFF:.2f}"`).[^stab] Neither is strong, and the early-down number, which comes from about four
times as many plays, does almost as well.

Second, **defensive third-down numbers are noisy.** A defense's third-down conversion rate allowed
carried over from one season to the next with a correlation of only `{python} f"{R_DEF:.2f}"`: barely more
than nothing. A defense
that "gets off the field" one year often doesn't the next, which is a reason to judge third-down defenses
on what they do (pressure, coverage, tackling) more than on the conversion rate alone. Offenses are more
stable, but the gap between the best and worst is still modest: in 2025 the best offense converted
`{python} pct(T25.max())` of its third downs, the worst `{python} pct(T25.min())`.

None of that makes third down unimportant; it makes it *consequential and noisy at once*, which is
exactly what you'd expect of a single high-stakes snap. [Expected Points, EPA, and Success
Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd) has the tools to measure it.

## Film room: the Patriots' option routes

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots 2009–2019 — Welker, Edelman and the sticks"}
The Patriots of the Tom Brady era built much of their third-down offense on slot receivers running option
routes set just past the sticks ([Passing Game Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)
and [The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd) introduce the route and Wes Welker). The
data shows what that meant on third down.

- **Wes Welker, 2009–2012.** Welker was New England's most-targeted receiver on third down in
  `{python} WEL_TOP` of those 4 seasons and the target on `{python} pct(WEL['share'])` of Brady's
  third-down throws to a named receiver. Those throws converted `{python} pct(WEL['conv'])` of the time,
  against `{python} pct(WEL['lg'])` for third-down targets across the league. And the typical Welker target
  was thrown **exactly to the line to gain**: the median distance between the throw's depth and the sticks
  was `{python} f"{WEL['rel']:.0f}"` yards. That looks like a contradiction: throws aimed right at the line are
the chart's weak spot. Welker beat the dip for the two reasons the dip exists. It comes from balls thrown
*into* a defender sitting at the sticks; the option route against zone finds the gap *between* two of them
and sits down in it, facing the quarterback. And it comes from defenders who have time to close; Brady
threw as Welker settled, before anyone could. Caught on the line with nobody in front of him, a receiver
only has to turn and fall forward.
- **Julian Edelman, 2013, 2016 and 2019** (the three seasons in which he played all 16 games; he missed 2017 injured):
  `{python} pct(EDE['share'])` of third-down targets, converting `{python} pct(EDE['conv'])` against a league
  `{python} pct(EDE['lg'])`.[^pats2]

Why did it work? Because the option route attacks the defense's third-down plan at its core. Against man
coverage the slot defender has to choose a side, and the receiver breaks the other way; against zone the
receiver sits down in the gap at the sticks, facing the quarterback. Brady could throw before the break was
finished, because he and his receiver read the same defender. **What to notice** on old Patriots third
downs: the slot receiver's first few steps are the same every time; the break comes at the sticks; the ball
is in the air before he turns.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Past the sticks?** On every third down for one half, make a prediction before the snap and check it
after.

- **Say the bucket out loud:** short (1–3), medium (4–6), long (7–10) or very long (11+). Then make the
  base-rate call: short, run or quick pass; medium, quick man-beater; long, a route past the sticks against
  pressure; very long, a safe completion or a draw.
- **Read the offense.** Did the best receiver move to the slot? Is the back still in the backfield (likely
  to stay in and block a blitzer) or did the offense go empty (five out, and the quarterback has to beat any
  extra rusher himself)?
- **Read the package.** How many defensive backs came on? Did a big tackle leave for a pass rusher? How many
  defenders are within five yards of the line, and how many deep? No deep safety means Cover 0; three or four
  deep with linemen standing up means the defense may drop eight. Then watch the quarterback point and shout:
  he is setting the protection's count, and the defense is trying to make that count wrong.
- **Find a spy.** Against a running quarterback, look for a linebacker or safety sitting in front of him
  who isn't lined up on any receiver.
- **Predict the target: past the line, or short of it?** Then, after the play, note where the ball was
  caught relative to the orange line, and who made the tackle.
- **For your log:** for each third down, write the bucket, your prediction (past or short), what happened,
  and the number of rushers. Over a game you'll see the defense's third-down personality (pressure,
  sticks, or both) and whether the offense's targets live past the line or short of it.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: third-and-3 at midfield"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-zero
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-3 near midfield. The offense is in 11 personnel, 2x2, with the back beside the quarterback. The defense has the Mike (M) and Will (W) standing in the A gaps, the nickel ($) pressed on H, both corners pressed, and both safeties (green rings) walked down to 6 or 7 yards."
dfn = four_down(ldt=-2.75, rdt=2.75) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, -1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, 1.0, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 0.9, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -3.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 0.9, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 0.9, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=55, to_go=3)
p.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 11.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=10)
plt.show()
```

**What is the defense likely to do, and what should the offense want to have called?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A Cover 0 blitz is the likeliest reading: man on every receiver, nobody deep, six or more rushing.**
Count the deep players: none. Both corners and the nickel are pressed, which usually means man coverage.
With the two linebackers mugged in the A gaps and both safeties walked down, the defense has up to eight
possible rushers and no one to protect against a long completion. That only makes sense on a
short-yardage down, which is where the league calls Cover 0 most (the Cover 0 section has the rates). It
could still be a disguise: one safety may bail at the snap into a Cover 1, and one of the mugged linebackers
may drop.

**What the offense wants** is a quick throw that beats tight man coverage before the rush arrives: a slant
from X or Z against an outside-leverage corner, a rub between H and the back, or a quick out. A run is live
only if the offense can account for the mugged linebackers, with a blocker for each of them, and against
this look the quick throw is the better bet. Even the quarterback sneak runs straight into the two
linebackers standing in its gaps; it becomes a better call once one of them shows he is dropping. What the
offense should *not* have called is a slow-developing route past the sticks: on third-and-3 it doesn't need
one, and against six rushers it won't get time.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: third-and-13 from the 20"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-drop
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-13 from the offense's own 20. The defense has four linemen down (E, T, T, E), one linebacker (M) at 7.5 yards, and six defensive backs: the nickel ($) and the dime back (D) 7 yards off the slots, the corners 8 off, and two safeties 15 to 16 yards deep, one on each half of the field."
dfn = four_down() + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.5, 0.8, "M"),
    D("NB", "NB", 7.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 7.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 15.5, 9.0, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.5, -9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=30, to_go=13)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 18.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
plt.show()
```

**How many will rush, where will the coverage sit, and what would you call if you were the offense?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely four rushers, with a two-deep coverage behind them and everything underneath sinking to
the sticks.** This is the third-and-very-long package: dime personnel, two safeties deep, corners off, and
only one linebacker. At 11 or more yards, defenses rushed exactly four on about
`{python} pct(DEF.loc['11+', 'four'])` of charted dropbacks in 2023–2025, so
the base call is four. Behind it, two safeties high usually means a two-deep zone (Cover 2 or quarters)
or 2-Man. Either way, expect the underneath defenders to drop to 12 or 13 yards, so that every route that
converts runs into a defender and every route that's open is short. Two catches: a simulated pressure
looks exactly like this until the snap (an end drops, the Mike or a defensive back rushes), and an end who
drops turns it into rush three. The picture tells you the distance-based call, not the exact one.

**The offense's options** are the third-and-long menu. If it wants the first down, the soft spot of a
two-deep shell is the middle of the field between and under the safeties, 14 to 18 yards deep: a dig or a
seam, thrown on time. If it wants the possession, the draw and the screen are built for this picture: a
light box, one linebacker who will drop, rushers chasing upfield. From its own 20, a 9-yard draw that sets
up a punt from the 29 is a reasonable outcome, and an interception at the 35 is the disaster to avoid.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-5 against a quarterback who runs"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-spy
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-5 at midfield; the quarterback is one of the league's best runners. The defense presses the corners and walks the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS) up on the slots, with one deep safety (FS). Four linemen are down, the Will (W) is at about 4 yards over the back, and the Mike (M, green ring) stands 6 yards deep, directly in front of the quarterback, lined up on no one."
dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.2, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.7, -3.2, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 8.6, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=60, to_go=5)
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 16.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=15)
plt.show()
```

**What is the Mike's job, what coverage is behind him, and where is the offense's best throw?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The Mike is probably a spy, in Cover 1.** Every receiver has a defender pressed or tight on him (the
corners on X and Z, the nickel on H, the safety on Y, the Will on the back), one safety is deep, and the
Mike is lined up on nobody, square to the quarterback at spy depth. Against a quarterback who runs on
third-and-5, the defense has given up its robber to keep him in the pocket.

**Where to throw:** not right in front of the spy. His eyes are on the quarterback, so he sees every throw
that crosses his face at 5 to 8 yards, and spies rob those throws all the time. The good throws are the
ones he can't get to:

- **Behind him and in front of the free safety:** a dig or an over route at 10 to 14 yards. In Cover 1 with
  no robber, that is the space the defense emptied, and the spy can't turn and run back to it while
  watching the quarterback.
- **Away from leverage, outside:** an out or option-out by a slot receiver whose defender is aligned inside
  him, toward the sideline the spy can't reach.
- **Make the spy choose:** send the back on a route right at him, or a receiver across his face, so that
  covering the route means leaving the quarterback.

And the quarterback still has his legs: a spy who is slower than him has to be right about the angle.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Third down decides drives**, about three points of expected value on one snap, and the league converts
  about two in five, every year. The distance is the whole story: short third downs are converted most of
  the time, very long ones rarely.
- **The distance is information, so both sides specialise.** Defenses add defensive backs and pass rushers
  as the distance grows; offenses set their routes by the line to gain, put their best receiver where he can
  win, count the protection, and keep a third-down back.
- **Aim a yard or two past the sticks.** Third-down throws aimed there convert most often; throws short of
  the line rarely do, except on third-and-short, in four-down territory, or when the yards after the catch
  are the plan. Option routes, rubs and mesh exist to win that yard against man coverage, which costs the
  defense flags as well as catches.
- **The defense picks a point on a dial:** Cover 0 and tight man on short yardage, pressure (real and
  simulated) and 2-Man on third-and-7 to 10, sticks defense and rush three/drop eight on very long, and a spy
  when the quarterback can run. Each call gives something up, none wins on average once the distance is held
  still, and the best defenses show the same look for all of them.
- **Third-and-long is often about the possession, not the down.** Screens and draws rarely convert, but
  they avoid disasters, shorten punts, and keep the rush honest for the next one.
- **Third down is consequential and noisy.** Early-down success predicts it nearly as well as past
  third-down success does, and defensive third-down rates barely carry over year to year.

[^swing]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons, every third-down run and pass (kneel-downs and spikes excluded): average EPA of plays that reached the line to gain or scored, against those that didn't. Plays wiped out by penalties are not included. The swing is larger in the middle of the field and smaller near either goal line.

[^conv]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2016–2025, every third-down run and pass (kneel-downs and spikes excluded); a conversion is a play that gained the line to gain or on which the offense scored (`third_down_converted`, or a touchdown by the offense; a turnover returned for a touchdown is a failure). First downs by penalty are not counted, which is why published rates that include them run slightly higher. The highest season was 2020.

[^buckets]: Same data and definitions as the season rates, 2021–2025 regular seasons. Dropbacks are nflverse `qb_dropback` plays: pass attempts, sacks and scrambles. Pass shares are the share of third-down snaps at each distance that were dropbacks.

[^sticksdata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons: third-down pass attempts with a recorded `air_yards` (sacks and scrambles excluded; throwaways usually have no charted depth). "At it" means air yards equal to the yards to go. Air yards are measured to where the ball was caught or would have been, not to where the receiver was tackled.

[^defdata]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` (FTN charting), 2023–2025 regular seasons, third-down dropbacks; man share among plays charted `MAN_COVERAGE` or `ZONE_COVERAGE`. The charters' man/zone split shifts from season to season, so treat the levels as rough and the pattern by distance as the finding.

[^defdata2]: Same data as the man-coverage shares. Defensive backs counted from `defense_personnel` (CB, S, FS, SS and DB entries); "dime or more" is six or more. Blitz is five or more `number_of_pass_rushers`; Cover 0 is a share of plays with a charted `defense_coverage_type`. Early downs are first- and second-down dropbacks in the same seasons.

[^nascar]: Jenny Vrentas, "Steve Spagnuolo: The Man With Four Aces Up His Sleeve," *Sports Illustrated* (Dec. 27, 2016): https://www.si.com/nfl/2016/12/27/nfl-new-york-giants-steve-spagnuolo-defensive-coordinator (the 2007 "Four Aces" package of four pass rushers). The "NASCAR" name for the Giants' four-defensive-end package on third-and-long: Bleacher Report, "5 Scheme Adjustments the New York Giants Should Consider in 2012" (2012): https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1177469-5-scheme-adjustments-the-new-york-giants-should-consider-in-2012 ; Justin Tuck after Super Bowl XLVI: "We came up with NASCAR; we call it our speed package" (to ESPN, quoted by Jayski, Feb. 7, 2012: https://www.jayski.com/2012/02/07/nascar-propels-giants-to-super-bowl-victory/). The SI piece names no players for the 2007 package, so neither does the text; [Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd) has the 2007 ends.

[^pats]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2018–2019 regular seasons: third-down pass attempts by New England with a named receiver (sacks and scrambles excluded). White led the Patriots in third-down targets in both seasons.

[^kc]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()`, regular seasons: share of dropbacks with five or more `number_of_pass_rushers`, by down; Kansas City's third-down rank among 32 defenses. 2020 for comparison: `{python} pct(KC20_E)` early, `{python} pct(KC20_3)` on third down (rank `{python} KC20_RK`). Cover 0 share of charted third-down dropbacks, 2025: Kansas City first (rank `{python} KC25_RANK`). Third-down conversion rate allowed from play-by-play (runs and passes, conversions as defined above). Spagnuolo as Chiefs defensive coordinator since 2019 and in 2026: this book's fact sheet of 2026 staffs. The 2024 Chiefs' 15–2 record: Pro Football Reference, https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/kan/2024.htm

[^mia]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()`: Cover 0 as a share of third-down dropbacks with a charted `defense_coverage_type`, by defense, regular seasons. 2020–2022 coverage labels come from NGS and 2023 onward from FTN, so seasons on either side of the break are not directly comparable; within-season ranks are. Miami 2021 rank: `{python} MIA21_RANK`. Flores's career (Patriots scouting staff 2004–2007 and coaching staff 2008–2018, Dolphins head coach 2019–2021, Vikings defensive coordinator from 2023): "Brian Flores," Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Flores ; his 2026 status, this book's fact sheet of 2026 staffs.

[^eisenberg]: John Eisenberg, "The Breakdown: Eisenberg's Five Thoughts on the Loss to Miami," BaltimoreRavens.com (Nov. 12, 2021): https://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/the-breakdown-eisenberg-s-five-thoughts-on-the-loss-to-miami ("The Dolphins succeeded in pressuring Jackson with a heavy diet of blitzes and a Cover Zero scheme"; "overwhelmed by relentless blitzes"). Score, records and the rush and coverage counts: course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and participation (NGS charting) for game `2021_10_BAL_MIA`; other counts circulated after the game (for example "31 of 50 dropbacks") use different definitions of a dropback and of all-out pressure. Eisenberg also gives Baltimore's third downs as "two of 14," as the course count does. Records going in (Ravens 6–2, Dolphins 2–7) and the 22–10 final: Pro Football Reference, https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/202111110mia.htm ; BaltimoreRavens.com game page, https://www.baltimoreravens.com/game-day/2021/reg-week10/ravens-at-dolphins .

[^rush3]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` (FTN charting) and play-by-play, 2023–2025 regular seasons, third-and-7-or-longer dropbacks by `number_of_pass_rushers`; conversion as defined above; sack rate is sacks per dropback. Team rates are shares of each defense's third-and-7-plus dropbacks with three or fewer rushers. Minter was the Chargers' defensive coordinator in 2024–2025 and Sheppard the Lions' in 2025 (and 2026); Minter's 2026 job and Sheppard's 2026 status: this book's fact sheet of 2026 staffs.

[^chenal]: Charles Goldman, "Chiefs' third-year linebacker sent a message to the rest of the NFL with his dominant Week 1 performance," *A to Z Sports* (Sept. 9, 2024): https://atozsports.com/nfl/chiefs-leo-chenal-sent-message-rest-of-the-nfl-dominant-week-1-performance/ (Chenal "lined up in five different positions in the box, two different positions on the defensive line, and as an overhang defender in the slot"; he kept Jackson from beating the Chiefs with his legs "in key moments"). Arrowhead Pride's film review of his role is at https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2024/9/14/24243203/chiefs-roster-leo-chenal-honored-expanding-role-defense . Jackson's carries, yards and scrambles, the third-down runs and the score: course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, game `2024_01_BAL_KC` (designed runs and scrambles; kneel-downs excluded).

[^sheppard]: John Maakaron, "Detroit Lions DC reveals when QB spy folder built," *Sports Illustrated* (All Lions, Sept. 25, 2025): https://www.si.com/nfl/lions/onsi/news/detroit-lions-dc-reveals-when-qb-spy-folder-built (reporting Sheppard's earlier public displeasure with spies, and his answer: "I wouldn't believe much that I ever say about schematic things in public"; also "I've had that QB spy folder built for three years"; "It's not because of a spy guys, it's because we're making everything look the same"). Score, sacks and Jackson's rushing: course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, game `2025_03_DET_BAL`.

[^stab]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2016–2025: team-season third-down conversion rate (runs and passes) and first- and second-down success rate, correlated with the same team's third-down conversion rate the following season (288 team-season pairs). The defensive correlation uses third-down conversion rate allowed.

[^pats2]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons: New England third-down pass attempts with a named receiver (sacks and scrambles excluded); league rate is all teams' third-down targeted attempts in the same seasons. Receiver names are missing from about four in ten 2007–2008 nflverse pass plays, so Welker's 2007–2008 seasons are left out. Median "throw depth minus yards to go" uses `air_yards`. Edelman's 16-game seasons: Pro Football Reference, https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/E/EdelJu00.htm . He missed the 2017 season with a torn ACL: "Julian Edelman," Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Edelman . The comparison is not adjusted for distance; Welker's and Edelman's targets came at slightly shorter average distances than the league's.

[^empty]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` joined to play-by-play, 2020–2022 regular seasons: share of dropbacks with `offense_formation` charted `EMPTY`, third down against first and second down. The formation labels in this data come from NGS charting through 2022; from 2023 the field records only shotgun, under center or pistol, so later seasons can't be counted the same way.

[^flags]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons: every third-down snap, including plays wiped out by a penalty (kneel-downs and spikes excluded), on which a penalty against the defense gave the offense a first down (`first_down_penalty`). The man/zone comparison joins 2023–2025 third-down dropbacks and penalty snaps to FTN's `defense_man_zone_type` and counts flags for defensive pass interference, defensive holding and illegal contact, accepted or not. Enforcement (illegal contact and defensive holding, five yards and an automatic first down; defensive pass interference, a first down at the spot of the foul, Rule 8, Section 5): NFL, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ , as set out in [Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).

[^twoman]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` (FTN charting), 2023–2025 regular seasons: share of dropbacks with a charted `defense_coverage_type` of `2_MAN`, third-and-4 to 6 and third-and-7 to 10 against first and second down.

[^c0long]: Course calculation from nflverse `load_participation()`: Cover 0 as a share of third-and-7-or-longer dropbacks with a charted `defense_coverage_type`, by defense, regular seasons 2021 (NGS labels) and 2025 (FTN labels); rank among 32 defenses within the season. Both teams also played Cover 0 more often on short third downs than on long ones.

[^scramble]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2021–2025 regular seasons: third-down dropbacks with `qb_scramble`, and the conversion rate of scrambles and of all dropbacks on third-and-7 to 10 (conversion as defined above).
